faq.a: The standard deduction is a fixed amount the IRS lets you subtract from your income before tax is figured. For 2026 it is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for married couples filing jointly, and $24,150 for heads of household. For 2027 it is $16,600 single, $33,200 married filing jointly, and $24,925 head of household. This calculator always uses the standard deduction. If you itemize, your tax will differ.
faq.q: What is the standard deduction, and does this calculator use it?

faq.a: Your marginal rate is the rate on your last dollar of taxable income. Your effective rate is your total tax divided by your total gross income, and it is always lower than your marginal rate when income spans more than one bracket. A single filer with $120,000 of gross income in 2026 has a 22% marginal rate but a 14.6% effective rate.
faq.q: What is the difference between my marginal rate and my effective rate?

faq.a: No. This is a federal income tax estimate only. It does not include state income tax, Social Security or Medicare payroll taxes, self-employment tax, or any credits such as the child tax credit. It also assumes you take the standard deduction and have no other adjustments.
faq.q: Does this include state tax, payroll tax, or tax credits?

faq.a: Yes. The 2026 figures come from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32, and the 2027 figures come from IRS Revenue Procedure 2026-35, published November 5, 2026 with news release IR-2026-133. The tax rates are the same in both years: 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37%.
faq.q: Where do the bracket figures come from?
